summary:
A planning tool for Mars astronauts. The crew picks a base camp and science stops around Mount Sharp in Gale Crater. The planner finds a walking route that avoids steep ground and draws a "turn-back line", the farthest the crew can go and still walk home in time. It gives a plain "Safe to go / Tight / Not safe" verdict and includes a solar-storm drill. A 3D drive mode lets users steer the crew's rover with WASD under real Mars gravity and park it where base camp should go.

It layers four kinds of real NASA data: imagery, elevation, weather and radiation. It focuses on astronaut safety and uses rover photos and a rover-based camp.

A Mars crew can't call for rescue, so every walk must be planned against limited oxygen, nightfall, rough terrain and radiation. This tool makes those trade-offs clear to non-experts, using data from a real site.
details:
Mars Explorer: A Mars EVA Planner

Plan a safe walk on Mars.

What it does

A crew picks a base camp and science stops on a 3D map of Mount Sharp in Gale Crater. The planner then:

  • finds a walking route that avoids steep ground;
  • checks it against life support and daylight;
  • draws a turn-back line, the farthest the crew can go and still walk home in time;
  • gives a one-line verdict: Safe to go, Tight or Not safe.

A solar-storm drill replays the real May 2024 storm. A drive mode lets users steer the crew's rover with WASD under real Mars gravity and park it where base camp should go.

Why Mount Sharp, Gale Crater

  • Science: its layers record how Mars dried out. Its boxwork ridges are mineral veins left by ancient groundwater, and sampling them would show when and for how long water flowed there.
  • Data: few places on Mars have so much, including 1 m elevation, 25 cm colour imagery, and Curiosity's own path, photos, weather and radiation readings.
  • Checkable: the preset stops are Curiosity's own drill sites, so our slope and tilt figures can be compared with what the rover measured.

Benefits

  • The crew sees at a glance whether a walk is safe, and why.
  • The wording is plain, and every number comes from real data.

Intended impact

  • A Mars crew can't call for rescue.
  • We want the limits of oxygen, nightfall, rough ground and radiation to be easy to see and act on.

Tools

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, numpy, scipy.
  • Frontend: TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, three.js.
  • Data: USGS, HiRISE, Curiosity.
  • Hardware: an ordinary PC and browser.

What is creative

  • One picture for safety: the turn-back line combines several limits into a single line on the map.
  • Real Mars physics: the rover uses Mars gravity (38% of Earth's) and a mass estimated for three crew. It brakes about 2.6 times farther than on Earth and drifts in turns.
  • Familiar layout: the screen copies a consumer maps app to make mission planning approachable.

Factors we considered

  • Safety first: time limits use whichever is tighter, life support or daylight.
  • Honest limits: the 1 m data can't show small rocks, and the rover figures are estimates.
  • Plain language: few controls, with details only when asked for.
  • Credit: all NASA and partner data is credited.
  • Correctness: tests check the maths.
